DUBAI, Sept 7 (Reuters) - Iran said it will announce a new restricted zone in the Gulf in the coming days, ​along with maps of a new shipping corridor through the Strait of Hormuz, as a weekend exchange of strikes on shipping sent oil prices higher on Monday.

The new restricted zone ‌will begin from where the U.S. blockade of Iran begins and extend into areas of the Gulf, Mohsen Rezaei, the secretary of Iran's Supreme National Security Council, said on Sunday in an interview with state TV.

Sign up here.

Few details were provided on the plan, but Rezaei said any ship entering the new zone would be added to a sanctions list.

In addition, maps detailing passage routes for the Strait of Hormuz, a vital energy conduit largely closed to tanker traffic, would also be approved soon, Rezaei said.

"The maps of a new international corridor ​which lies in Iranian and Omani waters and in which Iran will have management have been agreed and should be signed in the coming days," he said.

"We will only commit to the ​Strait of Hormuz being open when they (the Americans) stop the sabotage, threats and attacks on Iran," Rezaei added.

Six months after U.S.-Israeli strikes on Iran sparked the war, the ⁠conflict appears to be at a stalemate. A preliminary ceasefire accord reached in June has unravelled, and little progress has been made in diplomatic efforts to get the peace process back on track.

# Ukrainian strikes on logistics hubs disrupt Russian grain exports — Ivashchenko

Exclusive

Ukrainian strikes on logistics hubs have created problems for Russian grain exports.

Oleh Ivashchenko, Chief of the Defence Intelligence of Ukraine (HUR), said this in an [interview with Ukrinform.](undefined)

“The[strikes and the situation in the Black Sea are already creating additional problems](undefined) for Russia’s export logistics, particularly grain exports. It needs to export around 40 million tons of grain from this year’s harvest—by sea. This requires approximately 30 vessels every day. There are virtually no alternative routes. There are more expensive options, such as transporting grain by rail to Baltic Sea ports or by road. But that is not a solution to the problem,” he said.

According to the intelligence chief, Russia produces around 130 million tons of grain. It retains approximately 80 million tons for domestic needs, while the remainder is exported.

Russian grain exports are currently being obstructed because grain is also a state resource used to support the economy and continue the war.

“And we can see the results of this work [long-range strikes—Ed.]. We can see this effect in Black Sea logistics and Russia’s export capabilities as well. Russia is losing the sense that its rear areas are practically unreachable,” Ivashchenko said.

He emphasized that the task of Ukraine’s Defense Forces is to reduce the enemy’s ability to produce weapons, supply its troops

The reporting, credited to Ana Swanson, Paul Mozur, Tripp Mickle, and Keith Bradsher, traces more than $5.6 billion in advanced technology that moved from a California-based Inspur subsidiary called Aivres through Southeast Asia and, according to trade records, onward into Chinese hands between April 2024 and February 2026.
